stimulus.text:
In August 1801, thousands of people gathered at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, for a six-day camp meeting led by the Presbyterian minister Barton W. Stone. Preachers from Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist churches preached at the same time from different platforms, and people wept, shouted, and fell to the ground as they were called to convert. Estimates put the crowd at 10,000 to 20,000 people, in a state whose whole population was about 220,000.

At the same time, some educated Americans followed deism, the belief that God created the world and then left it to run by natural laws, with no miracles and no revealed scripture.
stimulus.source_note: Cane Ridge account drawn from the Disciples Historical Society, Cane Ridge Revival, and the Revival of 1800; deism defined in standard terms.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from accounts of the Cane Ridge Revival, August 1801.

primary_sources: Barton W. Stone, account of the Cane Ridge meeting, August 1801

stem: Deism and the revival religion of Cane Ridge differed mainly in that...

options.text: deists held camp meetings while revivalists worshipped only in churches.
options.misconception: The stimulus shows revivalists holding the outdoor camp meeting, not deists.

options.text: deists believed in many gods while revivalists believed in one.
options.misconception: Deists believed in one creator God, not many gods.

options.text: both agreed that miracles proved God’s power every day.
options.misconception: Deism held that God left the world to natural laws, with no miracles.

options.text: deists trusted reason, while revivalists stressed conversion and feeling.

rationales.D: The stimulus defines deism as a distant creator and natural laws, and shows revivalists weeping and converting.
rationales.A: The camp meeting was a revival event, not a deist one.
rationales.B: Deism holds one creator God; it is not a belief in many gods.
rationales.C: Deism denied miracles, so it cannot agree that miracles prove God’s power.
rationales.general:
1. The stimulus says deists believed God left the world to run by natural laws.
2. It shows Cane Ridge crowds weeping, shouting, and falling as they were called to convert.
3. One side trusts reason and a distant God; the other seeks personal conversion.
4. So the two differed on reason and distance versus conversion and feeling.
Remember: compare the two beliefs side by side, using what the passage says about each.
